statement: In a class of $40$ students, $23$ play chess, $18$ play go, and $7$ play neither game. How many students play exactly one of the two games?

choices.misconception: I found that 23 + 18 - 33 = 8 students play both games and gave that instead of the number who play exactly one.
I found the 8 students who play both and subtracted them from the chess players only, which counts the chess-only students.
I found the 40 - 7 = 33 students who play at least one game, which still includes the students who play both.
I added 23 + 18 = 41, which counts the students who play both games twice.

hints: First find how many students play at least one game.
Inclusion-exclusion links the two game counts, the overlap and the number who play at least one. Find the overlap, then remove it from the at-least-one group.
At least one game: $40 - 7 = 33$. Both: $23 + 18 - 33 = 8$. Exactly one: $33 - 8$.

solutions.reliable: Of the $40$ students, $40 - 7 = 33$ play at least one game. By inclusion-exclusion, $23 + 18 - (\text{both}) = 33$, so $8$ students play both. The students who play at least one game split into those who play both and those who play exactly one, so exactly one is $33 - 8 = 25$. Check: chess only $23 - 8 = 15$, go only $18 - 8 = 10$, and $15 + 10 = 25$. Transferable idea: draw the two-circle picture and fill in the overlap first.
solutions.elegant: Adding $23 + 18 = 41$ counts each one-game student once and each two-game student twice. The at-least-one total, $33$, counts everyone once. So $41 - 33 = 8$ play both, and exactly one is $33 - 8 = 25$, or directly $2 \cdot 33 - 41 = 25$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
